title: Fufu
subtitle: West African cassava dough
excerpt: Fufu is a smooth, stretchy starchy dough made from cassava flour and eaten by hand with soups and stews. It has no strong flavour of its own; it carries the soup. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: A staple across West and Central Africa. Traditional fufu is made by pounding boiled cassava and plantain. This recipe uses cassava flour for the home kitchen, producing the same smooth, elastic texture.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Best made fresh and eaten warm. Firms up on standing.

glossaryTerms.definition: Flour made from dried, ground cassava root. It absorbs boiling water to form a smooth, elastic dough. Sold as tapioca flour in some shops.
The Nigerian term for all starchy dough eaten with soup. A piece is pinched, rolled in the palm, dipped into soup and swallowed whole without chewing.

The dough should be smooth and pull away from the sides of the pan. If it sticks, add a little more flour and stir over heat for another minute.

items.prepNote: use cassava flour or tapioca flour if available; semolina makes a similar texture

content.text: Bring 700ml water to a boil in a medium saucepan. Add salt.
Reduce heat to medium. Gradually pour in the cassava flour (or semolina), stirring constantly with a wooden spoon to prevent lumps.
Keep stirring and folding the dough over itself for 8 to 10 minutes until smooth, thick and pulling away from the sides of the pan.
Wet a bowl or ramekin with cold water. Scoop the fufu in and invert onto a plate to form a smooth mound. Repeat for each portion.
Serve immediately alongside egusi soup, groundnut soup or any thick stew.

attrs.cause: Flour added too fast or not stirred quickly enough
attrs.fix: Add the flour in a slow, steady stream while stirring constantly. If lumps form, press them against the side of the pan.
Add boiling water a tablespoon at a time and stir over medium heat until the dough softens to the right consistency.

content.text: Fufu as a concept spans the continent. In Nigeria, traditional fufu is made from fermented cassava; in Ghana from cassava and plantain pounded together; in Cameroon and Congo from green plantain alone. The instant flour version is now used across the diaspora. Each country eats it with a different set of soups, but the technique of eating with the right hand, tearing, dipping and swallowing is the same everywhere.
